plain: How many requests arrive each second. Often shortened to rps. It is the main way we talk about load.
Short for requests per second — how many requests arrive each second.
How much work a block can handle before it slows down or starts failing. Measured in things like rps or operations per second.
An extra copy of the same block. Replicas share the load and help if one copy dies.
A block that spreads incoming requests across several servers so no single one takes everything.
A block that runs your application code and answers requests. You can run several and put a load balancer in front.
A fast store of recent answers. A hit means you avoid calling the slower database or API behind it.
The share of lookups that find an answer in the cache. Higher means fewer trips to the slow store.
A rule that stops two writers from changing the same data at the same time. Stronger locks protect correctness but slow writes.
A content delivery network: copies of files kept near readers around the world so downloads are fast and the origin stays quiet.
A waiting list of jobs. Workers pull jobs and process them. Good for bursts; does not keep a global order.
An ordered log of events that many readers can follow and replay. Use a partition key to spread load while keeping related events together.
A block that pulls jobs from a queue or stream and does slow or background work off the main request path.
Do the slow part later. Accept the request now, put work on a queue, and let a worker finish it.
Safe to retry. Doing the same request twice has the same effect as doing it once — no double send or double charge.
Stops calling a failing dependency for a while so your own service stays up. Often paired with a timeout and a fallback.
How long you wait for a call before giving up. Too short and you skip healthy work; too long and you hang.
What you do when a dependency fails or the breaker is open — for example skip ads and still show the page.
Jobs waiting in a queue or stream that workers have not finished yet. A growing backlog means you are falling behind.
The delay that 99% of requests are faster than. It catches the slow tail that averages hide.
A geographic location where a block runs, such as US, Europe or Asia. Users far from a region wait longer, and a whole region can go down.
How long one request takes from start to finish. Lower is better. A latency target is the most delay you will accept.
A slice of the data on its own node. Sharding spreads load; a bad key can leave one shard too hot.
Replicas are copies of the same data for capacity and failover. Shards are different slices of the data. You often use both.
A group of writes that succeed or fail together. Ledgers and multi-step money moves usually need this.
The field that decides which stream partition (or shard) an event lands on. Same key keeps order for that group.
Adding or removing instances as load grows or shrinks, up to a maximum you set.
A cap on how many calls you may make (or accept) in a time window. Third-party providers almost always have one.
Someone else's API — ads, payments, email, maps. You do not control its speed, price, or outages.
When two features run on the same block, a failure or slowdown in one takes the other down with it.
Turning one write into many updates (for example filling many users' feeds) so each read stays cheap.
One popular lookup key that almost everyone hits. It can overload a single cache or shard node.
